item.title: Nvidia's first quarter without Huang: $115.8 billion in, $130 billion guided, zero China assumed and a margin that falls to 71%. What the numbers say about 2027
item.description: The beat was expected; the shape of the guide was not. Nvidia is now telling investors that the next quarter will be bigger, less profitable per dollar and entirely ex-China, and that the founder is not coming back.
item.content:encoded:
The beat was expected; the shape of the guide was not. Nvidia is now telling investors that the next quarter will be bigger, less profitable per dollar and entirely ex-China, and that the founder is not coming back.

Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the quarter ended October 25, up 103% on a year earlier and 20% on the previous quarter, with non-GAAP earnings of $2.68 a share against the $2.47 analysts expected and a 74.9% non-GAAP gross margin. Data-centre revenue was $107.6 billion, up 110% year on year; the segment Nvidia now calls edge computing added $8.2 billion. It was the first set of results presented by Colette Kress, chief financial officer and interim chief executive since Jensen Huang resigned on November 12, and the first in which the company's forecast assumed nothing at all from China.

The guide, not the beat

Fourth-quarter revenue is guided to $130 billion plus or minus 3%, a figure that includes a fifty-third week in the fiscal calendar. The gross-margin outlook of 71% to 72% is the detail that matters. It is roughly three points below the quarter just reported, and at a $130 billion run rate three points is about $4 billion of gross profit a quarter that will go to memory suppliers rather than to Nvidia. Kress attributed the drop to higher component costs; high-bandwidth memory is the component in shortest supply, and its price is rising faster than Nvidia's.

The press release states that the outlook assumes no data-centre compute revenue from China. Tech Times, citing the call, reports that Kress said Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper products there, and that Jefferies puts the annual revenue forgone at $44 billion to $62 billion. Those figures are secondary; the policy fact is primary. The remote-access rule published by the Commerce Department on Monday closes the route by which Chinese customers rented Nvidia chips abroad, and Nvidia has chosen to forecast as if that route is gone for good.

The commitments

Purchase commitments, the contracts Nvidia has signed with its own suppliers, rose to $390 billion, up from the $279 billion disclosed in July. Neocloud commitments, the capacity Nvidia has agreed to buy back from the rental providers it invests in, stood at $32 billion. Nvidia returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the quarter and has $227.3 billion of repurchase authorisation remaining after the $150 billion increase approved in September; the company says it intends to use all of it by the end of fiscal 2028.

Read together, the numbers describe a company spending its balance sheet to lock in supply for a demand curve it believes is still steepening, while using the cash left over to support its own share price through a leadership crisis. Kress raised the annual growth forecast to 75% from 70% and said demand is accelerating.

The CEO question

Chair Harvey Jones said on the call that the board does not intend to bring Huang back and that the search for a permanent chief executive, covering internal and external candidates, will not be rushed. That ends a week of reports about allies lobbying for a return. Kress declined to discuss the circumstances of the departure. Nvidia's shares, which closed Monday at their lowest level since June 2025 and about 35% below the October 6 record, rose around 4% in after-hours trading.

The counter-argument

A guide that beats consensus by $20 billion while margins fall is the pattern that preceded every previous semiconductor peak: volume up, pricing power down. SemiAnalysis is reported to have cut its 2028 accelerator-spend forecast by 28% last week on slower revenue growth at frontier labs and tighter project financing. Nvidia's $390 billion of purchase commitments are a bet against that view, and if it is wrong the inventory charge would be historic. The Anthropic IPO prices tonight on exactly this question.

What to watch

The Senate Banking hearing on December 3, at which Huang and Commerce Secretary Lutnick have been asked to testify about export controls. Whether the permanent CEO is named before the next report in February and whether it is an insider. The first Vera Rubin volume-shipment disclosure. And the gross-margin line next quarter: if it lands below 71%, the memory suppliers, not Nvidia, are winning the cycle.

item.title: Corma's $125 million Series A at $1 billion, three months after stealth: what a 16x step-up on 25 people and undisclosed revenue says about the defensive-AI market
item.description: NEA has priced a defensive cybersecurity foundation-model lab as a unicorn before it has named a customer, betting that the autonomous attack tools in this week's threat reports create demand faster than compute can be provisioned.
item.content:encoded:
NEA has priced a defensive cybersecurity foundation-model lab as a unicorn before it has named a customer, betting that the autonomous attack tools in this week's threat reports create demand faster than compute can be provisioned.

Corma announced on Monday a $125 million Series A led by NEA at a $1 billion valuation, with seed investors Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue returning. The company came out of stealth on August 10 with a $60 million seed, so the step from roughly $60 million raised to a billion-dollar price took 13 weeks. Total funding is $185 million. Headcount is about 25, split between Tel Aviv and San Francisco.

What it sells

The product, Corma Workforce, is a set of agents built on a foundation model the company trained for defensive security rather than adapted from a general one. The agents connect to a customer's identity, cloud, endpoint, SIEM and firewall or intrusion-detection tools, take assignments over Slack or Microsoft Teams, run investigations and remediation, and present findings for human approval before acting. Chief executive Alon Pluda, a Unit 8200 alumnus, has recruited researchers from Google and DeepMind alongside offensive-security specialists.

The company reports deployments in healthcare, financial services, energy and critical infrastructure, retail and telecoms, with demand from Fortune 100 and Global 500 firms. One anonymised Fortune 1000 chief information security officer is quoted on a 94% reduction in end-to-end response time versus the previous provider. Corma's own figures are 99% of tasks completed autonomously, 100 times faster end-to-end completion and 95% lower cost per task, and it says it has expanded server capacity 24-fold and still has a waitlist. Pluda's framing is that model quality is no longer the limit; GPUs are.

No customer is named and no revenue figure is given.

Why now

The timing is not accidental. Google's threat group published its first documented no-human-in-the-loop exploitation framework on the same day. The FBI's flash alert on ARTEX agents reaching admin access in under three hours came on Friday. Pluda calls October's wave of breaches "Black October" and says it made the case for machine-speed defence impossible to ignore. Boards that read those reports want something that responds in seconds, and the incumbents are selling copilots.

The comparables

The nearest public peers are not startups. OpenAI launched two Daybreak security products on November 13 and sells GPT-6 Cyber to vetted customers at $20 per million input tokens; Anthropic sells Mythos to approved organisations. Corma's bet is that a model trained from the ground up for defence beats a general model wrapped in a vetting process, and that security buyers will pay for a vendor whose only business is theirs. Among private peers, Mirendil raised $1 billion at a reported $5 billion last week in eleven months; the pattern of enormous early rounds on thin disclosure is the pattern of this autumn.

The counter-argument

Every number in the announcement is the company's own. A 99% autonomous completion rate says nothing about the 1%, which in security is where the damage is, and "100 times faster" is measured against a human process the company chose. Twenty-five people cannot support Fortune 100 deployments across five sectors without heavy reliance on the customers' own tooling, which is also the integration surface an attacker would target. And a defensive model is a weapon with the sign flipped; the governance questions that apply to GPT-6 Cyber apply here.

What to watch

Named customers and a revenue disclosure at the next round. Independent testing of false-positive rates and action blast radius, the two numbers the announcement omits. Whether the platform vendors, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto and Microsoft, respond by buying a lab like this one or building one. And the compute constraint: a security startup that cannot get GPUs in Q1 2027 has the same problem as everyone else, with a louder customer base.

item.title: The Fed's Financial Stability Report: 87% of market contacts now name AI as the top risk, and $680 billion of computing debt is a third of investment-grade issuance. What the numbers mean before Nvidia and Anthropic report
item.description: AI has gone from a 30% mention a year ago to the single most-cited threat in the Fed's survey, and the report puts hard figures on the financing stack behind it: $1.1 trillion of outstanding public debt, up to $3 trillion of commitments not yet started, and close to $1 trillion of big-bank exposure.
item.content:encoded:
AI has gone from a 30% mention a year ago to the single most-cited threat in the Fed's survey, and the report puts hard figures on the financing stack behind it: $1.1 trillion of outstanding public debt, up to $3 trillion of commitments not yet started, and close to $1 trillion of big-bank exposure.

The Federal Reserve's semi-annual Financial Stability Report, released on Friday November 13, is the first in which artificial intelligence tops the list of risks named by the market contacts the New York Fed surveys. 87% of them cited AI-related risk, against 50% in the May report and 30% a year earlier. The next most-cited concerns were a broad correction in risk assets at 52%, higher long-term rates at 48%, and cyberattacks and fiscal sustainability tied at 43%. The survey ran in September and October, which means it closed before Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia, before the Anthropic prospectus and before the midterm elections.

Three channels, with numbers attached

The report groups its AI concern into three channels. The first is valuations: equity prices remain high, in the Fed's words partly on enthusiasm for super intelligence, and earnings that fall short could trigger a correction. The second is cyber, where the report names sophisticated state actors and, in a phrase worth reading twice, damage caused by frontier AI models themselves. The third is financing, and this is where the report adds data that was not public in one place before. Debt issuance tied to advanced computing reached $680 billion by October 2026, five times the total for all of 2023, and now accounts for nearly a third of nonfinancial investment-grade corporate issuance, up from under 6% three years ago. Outstanding public debt tied to advanced computing exceeds $1.1 trillion. Debt, guarantees and leases on AI infrastructure that has not yet commenced could exceed $3 trillion. The largest US bank holding companies have close to $1 trillion of exposure to large technology firms, data-centre developers, computing-related special purpose entities, private credit vehicles and utilities. The Fed compares the cycle with the late-1990s broadband and telecom build-out and says it may soon surpass it; the links among data-centre firms, public credit, private lenders and SPVs, it writes, create vulnerabilities that require close monitoring.

Why the timing matters

The report lands at the start of a week in which the two most important AI issuers price. Nvidia reports its third quarter on Tuesday with interim CEO Colette Kress presenting; consensus is about $108.8 billion of revenue, and the company's $500 billion-plus of third-party financing commitments is exactly the kind of off-balance-sheet structure the Fed is describing. Anthropic prices its IPO on Wednesday with a reported order book several times covered; its prospectus discloses about $901 billion of computing commitments, about $70 billion of them due within twelve months. The Fed does not name either company, but a reader can map its $3 trillion figure onto the disclosed commitments of a handful of firms.

The counter-argument

The case for calm is in the same report. Household and business debt vulnerabilities are rated moderate and the banking system sound. Investment-grade issuance by cash-generative hyperscalers is not 1999 telecom debt issued by companies with no revenue, and the $680 billion is spread across issuers with some of the strongest balance sheets in the index. A survey of 23 market contacts is a sentiment gauge, not a stress test, and sentiment that is 87% one way is often already priced. The Fed's own concern is less that the debt defaults than that it is interconnected: a bank lending to a developer, holding a SPE's paper, financing a private credit fund that lends to the same developer, and serving the utility that powers the site.

What to watch

Nvidia's Tuesday call for any change to its financing programme and lease guarantees, which are now a regulator's talking point as well as a governance one. Anthropic's pricing on Wednesday and whether the $26 billion placement from its suppliers is read as demand or as circular financing. The next FSR in May, which will show whether the 87% was a peak. For treasurers, the practical step is an exposure map: which of your vendors, lenders and counterparties sit inside the Fed's $1 trillion of bank exposure, and what happens to your cloud pricing and credit lines if one of them has to refinance in a worse market.

item.title: Mirendil's $1 billion Series A at a reported $5 billion, eleven months after founding: what investors are buying when they buy 'AI that does AI research'
item.description: A 5x step-up in five months with no disclosed revenue is a bet on a thesis; here is the thesis, the three claims that support it, and the two numbers that would prove or disprove it.
item.content:encoded:
A 5x step-up in five months with no disclosed revenue is a bet on a thesis; here is the thesis, the three claims that support it, and the two numbers that would prove or disprove it.

Mirendil announced a $1 billion Series A on November 12, led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital, with Google, Battery Ventures, Doerr Capital, Gil & Co, M13, Pear VC and S32 joining alongside existing investors. The company was founded in December 2025 and raised a $200 million seed in June, co-led by Andreessen Horowitz and Kleiner Perkins, at a valuation of about $1 billion. It has not disclosed the new valuation. A16z's jobs newsletter described the round as closing at $5 billion, and Bloomberg reported that figure in September as the target of the talks. No major outlet has yet confirmed it as the closed-round number, so we treat it as reported.

Who they are

The founders are Behnam Neyshabur, who co-led Google DeepMind's Blueshift team working on reasoning and mathematics for Gemini, and Harsh Mehta, who built the first version of Anthropic's internal research platform. Both joined Anthropic in late 2024 and left together in December 2025 with two colleagues, Shayan Salehian from xAI and MIT graduate Tara Rezaei Kheirkhah. Neyshabur's one-line pitch is that the most important application of AI is AI itself.

What they say they have built

Three claims support the valuation, and each is checkable in principle. Mirendil-Base is a coding model the company says one researcher, working with agents, pretrained from scratch in three and a half months for under $10 million of compute. Fern is a post-trained model with a context window the company puts at up to 10 million tokens. Lor, in private beta, is the product: a system that coordinates hundreds of agents to write code, design experiments, run them and iterate, which Mirendil says it uses daily for its own research. Compute comes in part from a Google Cloud agreement reported in August at more than $100 million, covering both TPUs and Nvidia GPUs; Google's presence in the round is not a coincidence.

Why investors paid up

The funding market has spent this year rewarding two kinds of company: those with revenue (LangChain's $300 million at $3 billion on 7,000 LangSmith customers, announced the same Friday) and those with a thesis investors cannot afford to miss. Mirendil is the second kind. If research agents can run the experimental loop of a frontier lab, the binding constraint on model progress shifts from researcher headcount to compute, and the handful of labs with thousands of researchers lose part of their advantage. Thinking Machines raised on a similar premise last year; Mirendil's twist is to sell the loop rather than the model. The round also lands in a week when Anthropic's IPO is reportedly covered several times over, which tells you how much capital is looking for AI exposure outside the public offering.

The counter-argument

The sceptical case is simple. Automated research is the claim every frontier lab now makes about its own internal agents. If the incumbents already have it, the market for a standalone research loop is other labs, and there are few of them. A 10 million token context and a sub-$10 million pretraining run are headline figures without published evaluations. And a $5 billion valuation implies a path to several hundred million dollars of revenue from a private beta product, in a year when two of the most capitalised labs in the world are about to be public companies competing for the same customers.

What the numbers would need to show

Two disclosures would settle most of the argument. A benchmark table for Mirendil-Base against open models of similar size, with the token count of the pretraining run, would show whether the cost claim is real or an accounting of marginal compute. And a named Lor customer running experiments it did not design would show the product generalises beyond its maker. Until then, this is a well-backed research lab with a strong team and a thesis, priced as if the thesis were proven.

What to watch

Whether Mirendil publishes evaluations for Fern and the base model before year end; whether Lor leaves private beta with pricing; and whether the Google Cloud relationship grows into the kind of compute commitment that would make Google both investor, supplier and, potentially, acquirer.

item.title: Nvidia approached Arm's Rene Haas, FT reports, as VCs count the 105 startup rounds Huang's Nvidia joined this year
item.description: The succession search is weeks from a decision at best; the money Nvidia poured into neoclouds and model labs under Huang may change faster than the CEO's office does.
item.content:encoded:
The succession search is weeks from a decision at best; the money Nvidia poured into neoclouds and model labs under Huang may change faster than the CEO's office does.

Two stories about Nvidia ran on Friday, and the second matters more to most readers than the first. The Financial Times reported that Nvidia's board has approached Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm, as a possible successor to Jensen Huang; Reuters could not verify it, Arm declined to comment, and Nvidia said it is still selecting a search firm and that speculation about any candidate, internal or external, is premature. Separately, TechCrunch gathered venture investors who put a number on what Huang's departure removes from the startup market: Nvidia took part in 105 funding rounds this year, often as the largest cheque.

The Haas approach, and why it is slow

Haas, 64, is a plausible name because he is a former Nvidia executive. He joined in 2006, ran the computing products business for seven years, moved to Arm in 2013 and has been its CEO since February 2022, taking it public on Nasdaq in September 2023 at roughly $54.5 billion. He also sits on SoftBank's board and since April has run SoftBank Group International, the unit that holds SoftBank's AI bets. Any move to Nvidia would mean untangling all three.

The FT described him as one of several candidates with no guarantee of an offer or an acceptance. Analysts quoted by Decrypt have also floated Nvidia's data-centre head Ian Buck and AMD's Lisa Su; neither is more than a name on a list. Inside Nvidia, Wired reported, a suggestion-box thread has drawn more than 1,600 comments, many asking the board to bring Huang back. That is a measure of staff sentiment, not of board intent. Arm's US shares closed down more than 5% and Nvidia's more than 3%.

The funding gap is already open

Under Huang, Nvidia behaved like the largest AI venture fund in the world. TechCrunch's reporting lists CoreWeave, Crusoe (including a $1.4 billion Series E), Mistral, Lambda, Black Forest Labs and an $800 million cheque into Reflection AI's $2 billion Series B before that company had meaningful revenue, alongside the pending $13 billion Hugging Face acquisition expected to close in 2027. Investors described a pattern: an infrastructure startup needing $100 million to $500 million of GPUs could raise roughly half of it from Nvidia at a $1 billion-plus valuation, and the deal locked the startup into Nvidia hardware.

Several investors said those decisions ran through Huang personally and that interim CEO Colette Kress is seen as more conservative. The expectation is smaller follow-on cheques and a narrower set of new bets. Battery Ventures' Dharmesh Thakker doubted Google, Amazon, Microsoft or AMD would write hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure companies the way Nvidia did; others argued the ecosystem is now bigger than one person.

The counter-argument

Nvidia's 8-K promised no change to the roadmap or customer commitments, and a board that just pushed out a founder over governance is unlikely to announce a strategy shift before earnings. Kress has co-signed every one of those investments as CFO. The venture pullback is an expectation, not an announcement, and Nvidia still has the balance sheet to keep investing if it chooses. The $500 billion AI data-centre financing pact announced in August has not produced deals, but that was true before Huang left.

What to watch

Tuesday's third-quarter call is the first with Kress alone and the first since Anthropic's prospectus disclosed a $10 billion Nvidia commitment; listen for the phrase 'strategic investments' in the guidance. Watch whether any Nvidia-backed neocloud reprices or delays a round in the next month. And watch Arm: if Haas is named, SoftBank has a succession problem of its own, and Nvidia would be run by someone whose last decade was spent making CPUs matter in AI servers.

item.title: Anthropic's IPO: China orders rebuffed, $900.9 billion in compute commitments and a '10th percentile' capacity plan. What to read before Wednesday's pricing
item.description: Six-times oversubscribed with a whole region excluded, and a CEO who says the hardest problem is guessing how many chips to buy: the two numbers that matter are $70.7 billion due by September 2027 and the spot market Amodei is relying on.
item.content:encoded:
Six-times oversubscribed with a whole region excluded, and a CEO who says the hardest problem is guessing how many chips to buy: the two numbers that matter are $70.7 billion due by September 2027 and the spot market Amodei is relying on.

Anthropic prices its initial public offering on Wednesday, November 18, and is expected to trade on Nasdaq as ANT the next day at $70 to $78 a share. Two reports on Friday filled in the parts of the story the prospectus leaves implicit: who is allowed to buy, and how the company thinks about the thing it spends most of its money on.

Who is in the book

Bloomberg reported that syndicate banks are refusing or discouraging orders from mainland Chinese and Hong Kong institutions, citing US International Traffic in Arms Regulations. Several banks have either declined the orders or told clients they are unlikely to get allocations. The amended registration statement says Anthropic's models, platform and applications 'may be controlled' under Commerce Department rules, including the Export Administration Regulations or ITAR, which is the legal hook. The same approach was used for SpaceX's $86.2 billion listing earlier this year, where investors in those regions could buy only once secondary trading began.

It has not dented demand. Orders are reportedly around six times the shares on offer. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley lead a 22-bank syndicate; the midpoint of the range implies a valuation near $1 trillion and roughly $61 billion raised, with a separate $26 billion private placement at the IPO price alongside. Anthropic emailed and then retracted an earlier version of the terms on November 9, saying the figures were inaccurate, before filing the $70–$78 range.

The compute dilemma, in Amodei's words

At a livestreamed conversation with Jamie Dimon at JPMorgan's headquarters on Friday, Dario Amodei called compute 'the deepest business dilemma that the company faces'. Buy too much and you overextend; buy too little and you cannot serve inference when demand arrives. His description of the policy is the useful part. Anthropic deliberately commits to a modest amount of capacity in advance, planning around roughly the 10th percentile of its growth scenarios, and buys more on the spot market when demand runs ahead. Spot capacity, he said, has always been there and he expects it to stay that way; he compared the approach to insurance and said the company wants to 'underpromise and overdeliver'.

The filing puts numbers on the modest end of that policy: $900.9 billion in compute-related commitments running to 2045, about $451.6 billion of it before 2030, and $70.7 billion due in the year to September 30, 2027. Compute costs reached 48% of revenue in one 2026 quarter. The prospectus does not name a backstop if spot availability fails.

The counter-argument

Planning at a low percentile and flexing on spot is what a disciplined operator does when hardware depreciates fast and demand is uncertain; the alternative, which some rivals have chosen, is to commit to everything and hope revenue arrives. If the spot GPU market stays liquid through 2030, and Nvidia's new management and the neocloud IPO pipeline suggest supply keeps coming, the policy looks prudent rather than fragile. Six-times coverage says most institutions have reached that conclusion.

What to watch

The print on Wednesday relative to the range, and whether the private placement participants, reportedly including Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC, are confirmed at the IPO price. The first-day trading on Thursday, with China and Hong Kong investors able to buy only then. The lock-up calendar, which determines when the $26 billion placement and employee shares can move. And one line in the first quarterly report as a public company: compute as a share of revenue. If it falls from 48%, the 10th-percentile plan is working; if it rises, the spot market is charging for the insurance.

item.title: Huang resigns from Nvidia: what the 8-K says, what the 14% intraday drop prices in, and why November 17 now matters more
item.description: The founder who ran the company for 33 years is gone with immediate effect, the CFO is running it, and the first earnings call without him is four days away.
item.content:encoded:
The founder who ran the company for 33 years is gone with immediate effect, the CFO is running it, and the first earnings call without him is four days away.

Nvidia filed a Form 8-K on November 12 saying Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer since 2013, is interim CEO and keeps the CFO job. Harvey Jones, the former Synopsys chief executive who has sat on Nvidia's board for decades, becomes the company's first-ever chair. The board says it will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent successor.

What the filing does and does not say

The 8-K gives no reason for the departure. It thanks Huang for 33 years, says the board has "full confidence" in Kress and the leadership team, and repeats that operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap continue without interruption. The resignation follows a week of reporting on Huang's personal relationships, including one with a senior executive who reported to him and alleged contact with a former Megaspeed executive accused of working for Chinese intelligence. Huang admitted infidelity on Sunday and apologised to employees. The board opened an independent investigation and says it has no reason to believe national security was compromised; no evidence has been published that company secrets were lost. Those allegations remain allegations.

The one hard date in the filing is unchanged: third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on Tuesday, November 17, at 1:20 p.m. Pacific, with the call at 2 p.m.

What the market did

Shares fell more than 14% at one point on Thursday before recovering some ground, on top of the 8.6% after-hours drop on Wednesday when the board meeting was first reported. US indexes closed lower. The intraday swing is the market trying to price two different things at once: a key-person discount on a founder-led company, and a political discount, because the reporting has pulled lawmakers into the question of how Nvidia's chips reach China. Semafor reported Thursday that there is "a high probability" Congress tightens export controls in response, and OpenAI publicly backed a set of chip-control bills the same day.

Three things that now hang on November 17

First, guidance. Kress has delivered the numbers on every call for a decade, so the figures will be familiar; what investors have not heard is her set the forward tone alone. Second, the Anthropic placement. Nvidia agreed to buy $10 billion of Anthropic's Class N stock at the IPO price, which is expected to be set on November 18. Al Jazeera reported the commitment is still expected to go ahead; the call is the obvious moment to confirm it. Third, Hugging Face. The $12.9 billion acquisition announced in September is still expected to close in 2027, and Hugging Face's chief executive said Thursday he will keep defending open-source AI. Any wobble on either deal would tell you the interim leadership is narrowing its ambitions.

The counter-argument

Nvidia is not a one-person company in the way the stock reaction implies. Its moat is CUDA, a two-year supply book and a product cadence that the data-centre and software teams run day to day. Kress knows every customer contract. Several analysts told Al Jazeera that investors were already rotating rather than panicking. Trump's public defence of Huang, and his suggestion of Tim Cook as a successor, also signals that the administration is not about to punish the company itself.

What to watch

The successor shortlist (Kress, Buck, Rene Haas, Lisa Su and Jones have all been floated); whether the 8-K's "no interruption" promise survives the earnings call; the Anthropic placement confirmation; and the first markup of the Chip Security Act or Remote Access Security Act, which would change how overseas GPU rentals are policed regardless of who runs Nvidia.

item.title: Nvidia's board weighs removing Jensen Huang: what an 8.6% after-hours drop and a $200 price target are pricing in
item.description: Five days before earnings, the world's second-most-valuable company may replace the only chief executive it has ever had; here is how to read the stock, the succession options and the export-control risk underneath.
item.content:encoded:
Five days before earnings, the world's second-most-valuable company may replace the only chief executive it has ever had; here is how to read the stock, the succession options and the export-control risk underneath.

Nvidia's independent directors met late on Wednesday, November 11, to decide whether Jensen Huang remains chief executive, according to Reuters, after the Wall Street Journal reported the board was preparing to remove him. Bloomberg reported the board is already working with an outside firm to identify candidates and is weighing an interim appointment while it searches. By Thursday morning no decision had been announced. The stock, which had closed up 2.9% at $173.73, fell 8.6% to $158.78 after hours and was down roughly 6% again in premarket trading.

How we got here in four days

On Sunday, November 8, the board disclosed an inquiry into whether Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation, after he admitted a relationship with a former executive at Megaspeed, the Singapore cloud company that rents Nvidia capacity to Chinese customers including Alibaba. US officials reportedly believe she worked for Chinese intelligence; China's foreign ministry called the claim groundless. The board expressed confidence in Huang that day and hired Wachtell Lipton. On Wednesday the New York Times reported, citing five current and former employees, a second relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice-president of healthcare, who reports to Huang. Nvidia and Powell did not respond. The second report changed the board's calculus from protecting a founder under foreign pressure to a direct-report relationship that most public-company codes of conduct prohibit outright.

What the stock is pricing

Nvidia has shed more than $450 billion of market value since the November 8 disclosure and is about 27% below its early-October high. Bernstein cut its target to $200 from $400 and Baird to $200 from $500 before any decision. Several banks estimate a further 20% fall if Huang goes; Dan Ives puts the company at $300 a share with Huang and $225 without. Those are opinions, not models, and they ignore the fact that AMD rose 3.9% and Broadcom 3% on the news, which says the market expects Nvidia's customers to hedge rather than buy less silicon. Alibaba fell as much as 7.1% in Hong Kong on fears that its Megaspeed-routed chip access draws new US scrutiny.

The succession problem is structural

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has run it ever since, and has about 60 direct reports. He told Bloomberg in 2023 that the company was built so that he knows how to run it and that he does not believe in succession planning. Under Nvidia's bylaws a majority of the 11 directors, all independent but him, can remove the chief executive with or without cause. Seeking Alpha reports chief financial officer Colette Kress is a candidate for interim chief. An outside appointment within days of a November 17 earnings report would be unusual; a more likely sequence is an interim chief from inside, a muted guide, and a search that runs into 2027. Elon Musk, whose companies are among Nvidia's largest customers, said hiring Huang would be an honour, which is the kind of remark boards notice.

The counter-argument

Nvidia's product cycle does not depend on one person in the way its culture does. Blackwell and its successors are committed, supply is contracted through TSMC, and the software moat is CUDA, not the keynote. On that view the 27% drawdown is already more than the governance risk deserves, and a clean leadership decision could be a relief rally. The risk that view misses is political: Senators Warren and Coons have asked Commerce, State and the White House to preserve records on Nvidia's China exports and the alleged intelligence operation, and a shareholder class action alleging investors were defrauded is already filed. Those run on their own clocks regardless of who is chief executive.

What to watch

A board statement, which could come any hour; whether an interim chief is named from inside; the November 17 earnings call and whether guidance is withheld; any Commerce Department action on Megaspeed or on rentals of restricted H100 and H200 capacity to Chinese customers; and the S&P and Nasdaq weightings, since Nvidia's size means its move is the index's move. For buyers of Nvidia hardware, nothing about allocation or pricing has changed this week, and the people who negotiate your contracts are not the ones in the boardroom.

item.title: Anthropic's IPO range is $70–78: what the amended S-1 says about dilution, lock-ups and the $26 billion partner placement
item.description: The largest technology listing ever attempted now has a price, a share count and a list of suppliers buying in; here is how to read the numbers before the stock trades.
item.content:encoded:
The largest technology listing ever attempted now has a price, a share count and a list of suppliers buying in; here is how to read the numbers before the stock trades.

Anthropic filed an amended S-1 and opened its investor roadshow on November 10, offering 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 each under the Nasdaq ticker ANT. At the top of the range the offering raises $64.4 billion, more than SpaceX took in June and more than any technology company has raised in a listing. The company has not announced a pricing date; FinanceFeeds and CNBC report trading could begin on November 19, while other outlets have earlier dates. Treat all of them as unconfirmed until Anthropic says so.

The share count, and what it does to the valuation

Of the 825 million shares, 801.4 million are new shares sold by the company and 23.6 million are sold by existing holders, so almost all of the money goes to Anthropic. Underwriters hold a 30-day option on a further 123.75 million shares. The $1.4 trillion figure that Fortune and others lead with is a fully diluted number at $78. On shares outstanding alone, the midpoint of $74 values the company at roughly $968 billion; adding options and unvested restricted stock takes the range to about $1.11 to $1.24 trillion. None of these is wrong, but they answer different questions, and a sell-side note that quotes one against another's revenue multiple is making an error.

The amended filing shows revenue of $17.0 billion for the quarter to September 30 and, per Fortune, an annualised run rate of about $81 billion at the end of October, up from roughly $71 billion in late September. On the fully diluted top-of-range number that is a little over 17 times run-rate revenue; on the midpoint outstanding-share basis it is closer to 12 times. Anthropic reported a first-half loss in its October prospectus and the amendment does not restate it.

The $26 billion placement

Alongside the public offering, seven strategic investors have agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting Class N stock at $74. Google and Nvidia take $10 billion each, AMD $2.5 billion, Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft $1 billion each and TSMC Partners $500 million. Combined with the IPO, Data Studios' reading of the filing puts net proceeds near $84.6 billion at the midpoint, or $93.7 billion if the option is exercised.

Every name on that list sells Anthropic chips, memory, foundry capacity or cloud. The placement locks in suppliers as shareholders and gives Anthropic a decade of negotiating leverage, but it also means that the public float will be a minority of the equity and that the most informed buyers in the book are also the company's largest counterparties. Class N shares sit outside the underwriter lock-ups but remain restricted securities.

Lock-ups and the overhang

Holders of about 15.5 billion Class A-equivalent shares are restricted from selling for up to 180 days. Co-founders and anyone holding more than 0.5% of the fully diluted count are restricted for up to 365 days. About 3.6 billion shares under the 180-day restriction can be released early if conditions in the prospectus are met, which usually means a price threshold after the first earnings report. For a stock whose free float at listing will be well under 10% of fully diluted shares, those release dates are the events that will move it.

The tape it is pricing into

The roadshow opened into the worst week for AI equities since spring. The Nasdaq fell 5.5% last week after the midterms raised the odds of tighter data-centre and AI regulation, and on November 10 Nvidia fell a further 5.5% to $168.80 on more than three times average volume after its independent directors retained Wachtell Lipton to run the investigation into reports that Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence effort. Microsoft briefly passed Nvidia as the second most valuable listed company. AMD and Broadcom rose the same day, which says investors see a Nvidia-specific problem rather than a demand problem, and both are in Anthropic's placement.

The disclosure nobody else has made

Buried in the risk factors is a statement that Anthropic's internal estimates suggest it "may imminently meet" the threshold in its Responsible Scaling Policy for dramatically accelerated AI progress, roughly a doubling in the pace of research because AI is automating it. The company says no current model has crossed the line and that it is considering policy changes to keep people in control of frontier development. In a blog post that would be marketing; in a registration statement it is a representation the company can be sued over. It is also a warning to anyone modelling Anthropic's costs that the compute budget is not going to flatten.

What to watch

The pricing date and whether the range moves; the final free float after the option; the first earnings date, because it fixes the early lock-up release; Nvidia's November 17 results, which set the mood for the pricing week; and whether any of the seven placement investors disclose offtake or purchase commitments alongside their stakes. If you hold OpenAI exposure through SoftBank, this is also the first public mark on the sector, and SoftBank's own shares will trade on it.

item.title: SoftBank's $7 billion loss lands on the day Anthropic starts selling a $1.1–1.3 trillion IPO
item.description: The largest outside holder of OpenAI just reported its first quarterly loss in two years, and the valuation range for Anthropic's listing has fallen for the third time in a month.
item.content:encoded:
The largest outside holder of OpenAI just reported its first quarterly loss in two years, and the valuation range for Anthropic's listing has fallen for the third time in a month.

SoftBank Group reported a net loss of roughly ¥1.1 trillion, about $7 billion, for the quarter to September 30, the company said on November 10. A year earlier the same quarter produced a ¥2.5 trillion profit, almost all of it an accounting gain on SoftBank's stake in OpenAI after a funding round lifted the private valuation. Three analysts polled by LSEG had expected anything from a ¥233 billion profit to a ¥113 billion loss; the actual figure was far outside that range.

Why SoftBank matters for AI

SoftBank has spent $64.6 billion to assemble a roughly 13% holding in OpenAI, which makes its quarterly accounts the nearest thing public investors have to a mark-to-market on the most valuable private AI company. When OpenAI's valuation rises, SoftBank books gains; when sentiment turns, as it did through a week in which AI stocks sold off after the US midterms and Nvidia's board opened a probe into its chief executive, the same line reverses. Reuters noted that SoftBank's own shares have roughly halved since early June. The group no longer holds Nvidia, having sold that stake in 2025, so its exposure is now almost purely to OpenAI and to the data-centre projects it is financing alongside it.

Anthropic's timing

The loss landed on the morning Anthropic was expected to begin formally marketing its IPO, fifteen days after its public S-1 filing, with investor meetings reportedly scheduled through the week and a Nasdaq debut possible before Thanksgiving. Bloomberg reported that investors now estimate a valuation of $1.1 trillion to $1.3 trillion. That is the third downward step in a month: $2 trillion was floated in early October, $1.4–1.5 trillion was the talk two weeks ago, and last week's reporting had buyers pushing back on $1.5 trillion.

The revenue line supports a large number by any historical standard. Anthropic's S-1 showed first-half revenue of $16.3 billion, roughly fourteen times the prior-year period, driven by enterprise coding use. But $1.1 trillion is still more than 30 times annualised first-half revenue, and the filing also disclosed around $895 billion of commitments, overwhelmingly for compute and infrastructure. Nvidia agreed last November to invest up to $10 billion, reportedly including a further allocation in the IPO, in exchange for Anthropic running its first gigawatt of capacity on Nvidia hardware.

The counter-argument

SoftBank's quarter is a lagging indicator of a sell-off that has already partly reversed; the Nasdaq recovered on Friday and Monday, and SoftBank's own shares rose sharply on the results day according to market data widgets, which suggests the loss was priced in. Anthropic also cut the price of its top model by 20% on November 9, which bulls read as confidence in volume and margin rather than a scramble for revenue. And the lower valuation range may be exactly what a successful deal needs: a listing priced to rise is better for a company that will return to the market for capital than one priced to the last private mark.

What to watch

The final price range, which should appear once the roadshow has a week of feedback. The lock-up terms and whether existing holders sell. Whether OpenAI, which has filed confidentially, accelerates its own timetable. And SoftBank's next disclosure of the carrying value of its OpenAI stake, which is now the public market's best read on what OpenAI is worth.

item.title: Anthropic's reported $3.4B generator buy makes power a capital expense for AI labs
item.description: Taking over 1.7 gigawatts of Caterpillar orders is the biggest known power-equipment purchase by an AI company. It tells you how the labs now think about the grid.
item.content:encoded:
Taking over 1.7 gigawatts of Caterpillar orders is the biggest known power-equipment purchase by an AI company. It tells you how the labs now think about the grid.

The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Anthropic agreed in late September to pay about $3.4 billion for roughly 1.7 gigawatts of gas-fired generators, taking over orders that OnePWR Solutions, a San Antonio power developer, had placed with Caterpillar about two years ago. The FT cited one person with knowledge of the deal; both companies declined to comment. We have not independently confirmed it, and the figures should be read as reported.

The structure matters as much as the size. OnePWR had the orders but needed capital to complete them. Anthropic had planned to buy power from OnePWR as a customer, then instead took over both the equipment orders and the installation work. No company was acquired and no staff moved. In effect, a model developer stepped into the shoes of a power developer because that was faster than waiting for one.

Why 1.7 gigawatts is a big number

A gigawatt is roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor. Today's largest AI training campuses are planned in the 1 to 2 gigawatt range, so this single order is on the scale of one flagship site's entire power budget. The FT described it as the largest known single purchase of power equipment by an AI company, a title previously associated with xAI's turbine deployments at its Memphis and Southaven sites, the Memphis installation having drawn a lawsuit over permitting and emissions.

The economic logic is straightforward. In most US markets, connecting a new large load to the grid now takes years. Buying reciprocating gas generators converts an open-ended wait into a delivery schedule, at the cost of owning a fleet of machines and the gas supply, air permits and operations that come with them. For a company whose amended IPO filing lists about $895 billion in commitments, almost all for compute and infrastructure, $3.4 billion to make a slice of that compute usable on time is a rounding error with outsized leverage.

What it signals about the IPO

Anthropic begins marketing its listing this week, and the S-1 has already been read closely for what it admits about energy. A frontier lab buying gas generation outright will be framed two ways. Investors will see a company securing physical capacity rather than relying on partners, which supports the revenue trajectory it is selling. Critics will see a lab that has talked about safety and responsibility choosing fossil generation at scale, days after voters in several states backed measures restricting data-centre development and after OpenAI pledged to cover the full cost of power and grid upgrades for its own sites.

Both readings can be true. The practical point for anyone modelling the sector is that power has moved from an operating cost that utilities deliver to a capital asset that labs buy, own and depreciate. That changes the shape of their balance sheets, the comparables analysts should use, and the political constituency the labs have to manage.

The counter-argument

Owning generation is not obviously the winning strategy. Gas prices are volatile, air permits are increasingly contested, and utilities in several states are moving toward tariffs that make large loads pay for their own grid upgrades, which would narrow the time advantage of self-generation. Hyperscalers with decades of utility relationships may still get to the grid faster than a lab with a fleet of Caterpillars and a two-year-old operations team.

What to watch

Where the generators go. Anthropic has not said, and siting will determine the permitting fight and the local politics. Watch for an updated S-1 amendment that reflects the deal, for Caterpillar's next earnings commentary on data-centre backlog, and for whether OpenAI, Google or Meta follow with equipment purchases of their own rather than power-purchase agreements.

item.title: OpenAI at $1.25T, Anthropic talked down to $1.2–1.3T: the week AI's two giants got repriced
item.description: Both labs are still worth more than almost any company on earth. What changed is that investors started setting the price instead of accepting it.
item.content:encoded:
Both labs are still worth more than almost any company on earth. What changed is that investors started setting the price instead of accepting it.

Two numbers landed within days of each other. On November 6 Reuters reported, and TechCrunch relayed, that OpenAI had closed about $11 billion as the first part of a larger round, at a valuation of roughly $1.25 trillion, with SoftBank and MGX among the participants. The company had reportedly been seeking $1.5 trillion. The same week, reports from Bloomberg and The Information described investors preparing for Anthropic's IPO roadshow, due to start the week of November 9, discussing a valuation around $1.2–1.3 trillion, below figures floated in October, with a smaller raise or a short delay both on the table if AI stocks stay volatile.

What is driving the discount

Three things converged.

Public-market volatility. AI-related stocks had a rough week, and public comparables are what IPO investors price against. A private round closed in a drawdown prices the drawdown in.

Capital intensity in plain view. Anthropic's S-1, filed October 26, put first-half 2026 revenue at roughly $16.3 billion alongside a very large net loss and multi-year compute commitments, including a reported ~$19 billion, 20-year data-centre lease. OpenAI has made comparable infrastructure pledges, including a November 5 commitment to pay the full cost of power and grid upgrades for its sites. Investors can now see the bills, not just the growth.

Adoption data. Ramp's spending index, reported by TechCrunch the same day as the OpenAI round, shows the share of US businesses paying for AI tools flattening after two years of growth. Plateauing adoption is survivable; plateauing adoption during an IPO roadshow is awkward.

What has not changed

Revenue growth at both companies remains extraordinary by any historical standard, and both rounds are still being filled. A $1.25 trillion valuation is a discount to a wish, not a crisis. The IPO itself is the first chance for the public market to price a frontier lab directly, and every private AI valuation on the street will be re-marked against where it trades in the first month.

What to watch

  • The amended S-1 with a price range: that is the moment the roadshow is real.
  • First-month trading in ANT, and whether OpenAI's remaining round closes at the same $1.25 trillion or lower.
  • Enterprise pricing moves from both labs over the next two quarters; pressure on valuation tends to show up as pressure on list prices.
